body: Amazon fell about **94% from 1999 to 2001** and took about a decade to regain its peak ([CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2018/12/18/dotcom-bubble-amazon-stock-lost-more-than-90percent-long-term-investors-still-got-rich.html)). Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia each fell more than 80% at some point ([Irish Times](https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2025/06/17/the-agony-and-the-equity-most-stocks-fall-more-than-50-at-some-point)). The median dot-com tech IPO, however, ended down 85% and never recovered ([Lambda Finance](https://www.lambdafin.com/articles/tech-ipo-drawdown-history)). "Hold through the drawdown" is good advice only when you understand the business well enough to tell an Amazon from the median IPO. Recovery arithmetic is unforgiving: a 50% loss needs +100% to break even, and a 90% loss needs +900%. With leverage, a drawdown you could have waited out ends with your position sold for you. That is the thread running from LTCM and Archegos to Buffett's remark that LTCM "risked what they did have and did need" for money they didn't need ([Novel Investor](https://novelinvestor.com/buffetts-lessons-long-term-capital-management/)).
